This was going to solve the problems of all those people who werfe over pensionable age and who could not manage on $75 a month.
Maybe this was believed by some Liberal candidates, but the immediate reaction of Premier Roblin of Manitoba was: What is there new in this? Such a plan has been in operation in Manitoba for the past five years. In the province of Alberta-and I am speaking subject to correction-we have had a program for the last four years called the social allowance plan, under which additional payments are made to deserving persons-to the blind, the disabled, the necessitous-according to need. I am informed by my hon. friend from Perth (Mr. Monteith) that throughout Canada there now exists provision for a good deal of the assistance provided for by the Canada Assistance Plan. In effect, the federal government is bound to share on a fifty-fifty basis the cost of any assistance given by provincial administrations in excess of the statutory limits.
What do we find here in the Canada Assistance Plan-this bold, new departure? Pretty well the same thing, though there are some minor modifications. Instead of pensions to the blind, pensions to the disabled and so on, we are to have Canada assistance allowances or something of that kind. This is

They deal with what is known as Bill C-146-the famous opting out bill. This was to be the breakthrough in dominion-provincial relations. Never once during the election campaign was mention made of this subject. I am informed that there is only one province which may have taken advantage of this legislation. I say "may have done so"; we do not know, and we do not know to what extent. Certainly none of the provinces outside Quebec have done so, according to information given to me by a number of provincial cabinet ministers. I well remember the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) saying that the government had laboured mightily like a mountain and brought forth a mouse. I do not know that there is even a mouse. It may have been entirely stillborn.
The Speech from the Throne was singularly silent on the subject of veterans affairs. I have only a passing comment to make in this regard. This afternoon the minister mentioned the Woods committee which is studying the workings of the Canadian Pension Commission. We are now near the end of January. I recall some brave words by the minister when last September he announced the formation of the Woods committee and said it would be reporting within three months. I should like to know when this committee will, in fact, be reporting. Of course, it was wrong to suggest that such a committee would report within three months. There is far too much to be done. Yet the country was given this lighthearted assurance by the minister that the work could be completed within that time.
Another question I should like to ask the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Teillet) is this: What about departmental re-organization? We hear rumblings of sweeping changes

in the department. What are they to be? It is true that as time goes on re-organization can be carried out. But there is one thing which no hon. member of this house would wish to see, and that is a re-organization of the department which would result in a decline in the service available to veterans, whether in the field of pensions, in the field of welfare or in the administration of the Veterans Land Act. There is far more involved in the Department of Veterans Affairs than mere efficiency.
I had a few months of experience following my hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) in the administration of this department. We certainly came face to face with the concept that a good deal of our veterans legislation cannot be interpreted merely on the basis of the letter of the law. A great deal more understanding is required-a great deal more judicious interpetation in this particular field.

What about the inadequacy of the 10 per cent increase in pension rates, as of November 1964, referred to by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) this afternoon? That again must be attended to by the government. We know that within the last three years there has been almost a 10 per cent increase in the cost of living which, in effect, has wiped out the 10 per cent increase that was granted to pensionable veterans in 1964.
Among the departments the creation of which is being forecast, we have one for manpower. It will be interesting to understand the thinking of the government in organizing this department, in stripping the Department of Labour of many of its functions, in taking immigration into the area of manpower, and saying how the department will plan on dealing with problems of labour mobility and the availability of labour in Canada.
On another occasion I shall want to go into some of the principles that are being used by officials of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration in dealing with self-sponsored

immigration, for example, when we are looking for the operators of textile machines. We are told that they must speak either English or French, and must have the equivalent of grade 10 education in Canada. These are the criteria that are being used against the applications of self-sponsored immigrants in certain fields of industry.
Hon. members will readily realize that nowhere in Canada do we have such restrictions for our native born people. Do these restrictions concerning grade 10 education apply to potential workers from the textile areas of Great Britain? Not a bit of it. Do they apply to textile operators coming from Germany? Not a bit of it. This is designed to get at certain people who would come from Italy and Hong Kong, people who are just as fully skilled.
Throughout Canada there is any number of textile plants where the labour forces are made up of people whose ethnic origins are as legion as the colours in Joseph's coat, where there can be 20 different languages used by the members of one work force, and yet they get along. There are no difficulties. These people can be trained just as well as anybody else; in fact in this regard they are better workers than a good many of our own Canadian workers. We will want to find out what is being done in this regard, and also in regard to the highly publicized campaign for getting skilled workers from western European countries. I am sure the former Minister of Immigration, who is now Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson), was literally as popular as the proverbial skunk in a henhouse when he went to those countries, which themselves are extremely short of skilled labour, and said, "We are coming here to take your skilled workers away from you."
There are many areas in Canada that are terribly short of skilled workers. We cannot supply them from our own sources, so we shall have to get them from other countries.
I say we must get the raw material for skilled workers. I venture to say we shall have to inaugurate a program of taking unskilled workers from some European countries, bringing them here and training them in our ways and skills. We shall need to do that if we are to fulfil the requirements for skilled labour.
I shall also want to discuss with the minister some of the problems concerning the transportation of workers within Canada. I have before me a report signed by Miss Ida H. Burns, dealing with a southern Ontario

Another point I wish to mention was referred to this afternoon by my colleague from Northumberland. I am glad the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) has indicated that some sort of conference is going to be held by federal and provincial authorities to deal with the tightening up of security transfers and security loans.
Across Canada during the past year we have had some regrettable incidents concerning fraudulent practices by corporations and individuals acting on their behalf, and I am sure more are going to be disclosed. This has been in the field of securities, and not only does it give a black eye to Canada in the foreign investment market but also causes a great deal of loss and hardship to Canadian investors. As a matter of fact I think in some ways that Canadian investors, who are traditionally accused of shying away from the equity market, are simply scared to go into it because of the practices that have been carried out and that have been permitted to take place.
The minister did not say when this conference will be held but I would hope to see it convened at the earliest possible date. I join my colleague from Northumberland (Mr. Hees) in commending the administration of the province of Ontario for bringing forward certain changes in this field. We have

I am not trying to be a prophet of gloom in this regard, but I am warning that unless adequate steps are taken and people are made aware of what is happening, we are in for some rough bumps in relation to the maintenance of industrial activity in this country during the next several months.
There has been a very definite tightening up in the money supply. Some of that tightening up has been caused by the Atlantic Acceptance Corporation bubble, together with the British Mortgage and Trust debacle. That was the time of both the Atlantic Acceptance Corporation bubble, as I like to call it, and the failure of the then Minister of Finance to indicate that near banks were going to be taken in under the supervision of the Bank Act. Something must be done in this sector or we are going to see a repetition of that Atlantic Acceptance debacle.
This whole thing was like a large rock being dropped in a pool: It had ripples which travelled all around. I am just wondering whether this is what the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) was referring to at his nomination meeting on September 30, and on a subsequent occasion by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer), when they said that the reason they had to have a majority government was that a certain number of restrictions and unpopular measures would have to be brought forward. Was tight money one of the things the Minister of Industry and the Minister of National Defence referred to?
We know for instance, that the interest on prime commercial paper is now at 4f per cent, or higher than it was in April when it

was below 4 per cent. We know that the rate for 90 day treasury bills has gone beyond 4.15 per cent, which is its highest level since 1962. We know that the rate for loans to investment dealers has climbed to almost just under 4 per cent and that in order to ration credit and curb loan demand the chartered banks are raising interest rates. I have a copy of a letter which indicates that this is being done.
Money supply, which had increased 12 per cent over the past 12 months, is now being reduced. There was some danger in that regard, but it is now being reduced. We know there is some difficulty regarding interest rates. We are not free to handle our interest rates because we have an accord with the United States, entered into by the former Minister of Finance, which will not allow our interest rates to go beyond a certain point above the United States rates, because we might cause that country certain foreign balance of payment problems as money comes from the United States to Canada.
We have undertaken to limit our foreign exchange reserves to a certain level. Are we now in Canada caught up in a problem regarding the foreign payments of another country and unable to deal with a situation which exists in Canada?
Let me speak about inflation, which is another thing that was completely disregarded in the Throne Speech. It was completely silent about how the government intends to deal with this problem of inflation, and certainly it is a pressing problem. I have before me a weekly bulletin of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics dated January 14, 1966 which states:
Canada's consumer price index reached 140.8 at the beginning of December, up by 0.4 per cent from the November index of 140.2 and 2.9 per cent higher than the December 1964 index of 136.8.
In other words, it is almost 3 per cent over last year, and we know that in 1964 it was almost 3 per cent higher than in 1963.
We see that the consumer price index in December of 1965 was 140.8, while in December of 1964 it was 136.8. The wholesale price index is just as important, if not more important than the consumer price index. The general wholesale index is as follows: On the basis of the 1935-39 index at 100 per cent, it rose to 253.8 in November, up 0.7 per cent from the October index of 252.0, and 3.6 per cent above the November, 1964 index. This gives an indication of creeping inflation
January 26, 1966
If one refers to the cost of buildings he will see that this is going up. In this regard I can tell you that the tenders coming into the Builders Exchange in Edmonton, and I am sure this is a reflection of what is happening all across the country, were coming in at 16 per cent to 25 per cent higher last October and November than in the year previous. I refer to tenders on long term contracts for 1966-67.
In reference to built-in wage increases, the full impact of wage negotiations involve a 3.6 per cent levy on earnings, up $5,000 by Canada Pension Plan, increases in commodity prices and building materials. We are still feeling some of the effects of the 11 per cent increase in sales tax on building materials and production machinery. In this regard why should we not expect a retrenchment in major capital investment in the building of new factories, offices, highways and all kinds of other enterprises?
The newspapers in the cities of this country are full of reports that various municipal authorities, school board authorities and hospital authorities are receiving bids and estimates far in excess of what they expected. They can have but two alternatives, not build or increase taxes. They must seek more money if they are to go ahead with their plans. Surely this is an indication of inflation.
Can we counter these effects of domestic inflation by our commercial trade as it stands? The answer is no, because if we look at the D.B.S. report of January 7, 1966, we will see that our commodity exports have been declining relative to our imports. Canada's domestic commodity exports were valued at $701 million in September of this year. This reflected a decrease of 3.2 per cent from the September 1964 total of $724 million. This placed the value in the January-September period at $6,058 million, which represents a slight rise of .9 per cent from the comparable year earlier. This decline in the value of commodity exports was due primarily to a drop in volume as that index fell to 206.4 from 216.1 a year earlier.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
If we look at returns for January 14, we will see the picture of commodity imports. Canada's commodity imports in August of 1965 were valued at $660,635,000, an increase of 16.7 per cent from the August, 1964, total of $566,165,000. This placed the value in the January-August period at $5,464,353,000, higher by 11.4 per cent than the corresponding 1964 total of $4,905,710,000. Mr. Speaker,
The Address-Mr. Lambert this is an indication of some of the problems we are facing. There is inflation, not only creeping but steadily advancing to inflation in this country.
Our productivity is down; our costs are up. We are exporting relatively less, and importing more. This is nothing but a foolhardy policy, and the people of Canada look to the government to deal in part with this problem. I will not say that the government is entirely responsible for this situation, but it must share the responsibility. After all, the government claimed the credit when the movement was reversed, so now it must accept part of the blame.
I want to commend to hon. members the steps outlined by my colleague the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees) showing what was done by the previous administration to stimulate international trade a few years ago. Those steps can be repeated; a number of them must be repeated. We in Canada cannot sit back and expect people to come and buy our goods. We have to get out and sell; we have to be keen, hard-nosed, in so far as our selling practices are concerned. People must be prepared to go out, get turned down and go back again-and they must have sharp pencils.
All of us, whether in government, management or labour, must remember that today price competition is really keen. You can talk all you want about the activities of economic councils, productivity councils, planning and incentives, but if you do not sell the goods that you produce, you have engaged in an exercise of national futility. Those goods must be sold. This is something that, unfortunately, far too many Canadians have forgotten.
I am going to advocate in closing, Mr. Speaker, one step to deal with inflation. I do not like price controls; they engender more problems than they cure. I am going to suggest something that it is within the power of the government to do. It is something they did which in part has caused prices to go up.
I refer to the 11 per cent sales tax on certain building materials and production machinery.
I was glad to see that one of the new members, the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Faulkner), who comes from a community that is vitally affected by industry, yesterday advocated the removal of the 11 per cent sales tax on production machinery.
Ever since this government came into office they have been told on very many occasions that this tax should be removed, and I am

January 26, 1966

The Address-Mr. Greene sure that in their heart of hearts they would like to do away with it. We give them the opportunity. This is the burden of my amendment. This is the first step that the government can take, namely remove this tax. I am sure if this were done it would remove at least one area of pressure in the inflationary trend in this country.

Now, Mr. Speaker, in attempting to answer some of the views, criticisms and suggestions that were made by members on all sides of this house, I find that I cannot cover the entire gamut of all the speeches. I shall try, to the best of my ability, to cover what appeared to be some of the salient points raised by hon. members.
First, I should like to refer to the address of the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Horner), who spoke with that restraint for which he is known in this house. The hon. member referred to departmental emasculation, troikas and such other controversial agricultural topics. At my stage of development in this game, I am afraid I am not qualified to reply to these more sophisticated approaches to agriculture. However, I do wish to respond to one point which the hon. member made concerning the question of emergency assistance in the Peace River area. This problem has been mentioned by several other members, including the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) whose presentation of that question was able and forcible.
I may say that other members on both sides of the house, including the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson), have drawn this very serious question to my attention.
I should like for a moment to deal with this question. I do not pretend, in the short time I have held this office, that I have become as expert on the question of P.F.A.A. as some members opposite. However, I should like to review momentarily the question of P.F.A.A. and the constitution of P.F.A.A., and to point out to this house the difficulties involved in rendering emergency assistance over and above P.F.A.A. to any P.F.A.A. area.
I point out, first of all, that this act, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, was first introduced in 1939 and has played a very substantial and important part in the agricultural problems of the prairie provinces. At that time, in 1939, the prairies had just come through nine years of drought and fairly general crop failure. As a result of the reduced income of the prairie farm population, the provinces faced a constitutional responsibility to provide relief assistance to thousands of farm families. I feel this is the essential point we must bear in mind, that this responsibility for relief lay, constitutionally, with the provinces. There was, and is, no authority in the federal government except as envisaged by a program of wide application such as P.F.A.A.
DEBATES	289
The Address-Mr. Greene
Obviously, in this post-1939 era, the provinces could not afford to set up any pervasive program which might help farmers in future situations such as those which had occurred in the past nine years. They therefore came to Ottawa with their program. As I have said, the ^responsibility for direct relief falls to the provinces. It was not appropriate, therefore, for the federal government to make relief payments to farmers on an individual basis. The only proper way that the federal government, constitutionally, could enter into the matter was on the basis of widespread crop failure. Then we came to the area of our constitution which the courts have defined as catastrophe or national calamity. It was, I believe, under this aegis of federal authority that we were able to enter this field at all.
I may say that it was a great pleasure for me to read the speech of the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Fane) in Hansard. I must apologize to those members whose speeches with regard to agriculture I did not hear at first hand, but I could not be in the house all the time. I assure them I have read everything that has been said by any member with regard to the topic of agriculture. I was pleased to read the speech of the hon. member for Vegreville who was in the next office to me in the West Block not long ago and with whom, in the traditions of this house, despite our political differences, I have been fortunate enough to reach a very happy degree of friendship. I was, as I say, happy and pleased to read his words, even though I cannot say that I agreed with all of them.
The hon. member pointed out that the townships in western Canada are six miles square and that originally the Prairie Farm Assistance Act provided there must be a crop failure in a minimum of something over 100 townships before the act became operative. We can see that, with a failure on that scale, constitutionally it could be argued that this would be a catastrophe in the nature of a national catastrophe which would give the federal government legislative authority. There were crop failures on the prairies in 1942, for example, but no payments were made under P.F.A.A. because the areas of failure did not reach these minimum requirements. It is interesting to note that the provinces, therefore, absorbed all the cost of any assistance provided. I mention this to emphasize again that the federal government has no constitutional authority to take over this area of relief, unless the crop failure amounted to
290	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Greene a national emergency and the area concerned was such as to amount to a national emergency.
Over the years there have been changes in the act to make it possible for a greater percentage of farmers affected by crop failure to participate in the benefits of this legislation. The minimum size of the crop failure area necessary to qualify for assistance now is 12 sections, or one third of the average township. I believe we have improved the area in which the federal department can be of help to this degree. At what stage we are encroaching upon provincial powers is probably a moot point. Certainly we have made improvements up to this point without receiving any serious constitutional objections.
Again, the hon. member for Vegreville suggested in his speech that these minimum areas should be reduced, possibly to one section which would equal one square mile. Other suggestions have been made, of course, that eligibility for assistance under the act should be provided on an individual farm yield basis. Here again we get to the point that, that while this may be a desirable end, when we reach areas of this small magnitude we are not clearly encroaching upon provincial powers and provincial responsibilities. It would be difficult to argue that areas this small would constitute something in the nature of national tragedy or catastrophe whereby we could constitutionally enter the field.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
This is one of the reasons why the federal government is so anxious to see the provincial governments push ahead with crop insurance. Crop insurance can be made available on an individual farmer basis and the farmer himself can decide just how extensive he wants his production protection to be. Nevertheless, officials of my department have been giving considerable study and thought particularly during the past summer, to possible amendments to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act which would meet criticisms now directed toward it and still be constitutionally acceptable. This is a difficulty, but it is certainly my great hope, as I know it is of most of the members involved in these questions, that crop insurance, when brought forth and pushed to its ultimate limit, will relieve so many of these areas where help at the federal level does not seem to be constitutionally possible. We hope to discuss some of the

DEBATES	January 26, 1966
thoughts which have developed along this line with the provincial and municipal authorities concerned on the prairies.
There has also been some indication from comments during this debate that there is some misunderstanding about the federal government's contribution toward P.F.A.A. payments. Farmers contribute to the cost of this program by putting a 1 per cent levy on the amounts they receive for grain delivered to licensed dealers. This money is put into a fund known as the prairie farm emergency fund. It is from this fund that all P.F.A.A. payments to farmers are made. However, there is also a provision that when the farmers' contributions do not amount to enough to cover P.F.A.A. payments, the federal government will make up the difference.
I think hon. members will be interested to know that in the period from 1939 to July 31, 1965 farmers in the three prairie provinces paid about $164 million into the fund, while during the same period they have collected some $353 million; or, in other words, $189 million more than they have paid in, which, of course, has been contributed by the federal government. That is to say, for every dollar which the prairie farmers have paid into the P.F.A.A. emergency fund up to last July, they have been paid back more than $2. The people of Canada, through the federal government, have thus contributed since 1939 some $189 million to the prairie farmers through P.F.A.A. over and above the contributions made by the farmers.
In the light of this it is very difficult for me to understand the fairness of the criticisms which have been made with respect to our stand in this matter-criticisms that the western farmer has been discriminated against- when payments of this magnitude have come from the federal treasury.

We recognize that there will always be room for improvement. I believe that this act has materially relieved provincial and municipal governments in the three prairie provinces from the burden of crop failure relief to farmers during the 27 years since its inception.
I cannot help but compare the federal relief assistance in this way for so many years to provincial and municipal governments on the prairies with the rarity of this kind of federal farm relief in eastern areas such as the Ottawa valley, where no such
January 26, 1966	COMMONS
program has been available over this period of time. Nevertheless, we in my department have given and are continuing to give every consideration we can to the plight of farmers in certain areas of Alberta at the present time. There are many difficulties involved in the P.F.A.A. program not all of which are the concern of the federal government. Under the act the first responsibility for applying for P.F.A.A. payments rests on the local or provincial government. Counties, municipalities, and in the case of unorganized or local improvement districts, the provincial governments, are required to act under the act to make application for assistance in areas which they consider to have experienced crop failure. These initial applications are to be made before September 15 in each year, and the act becomes operative in areas where expected yields are below eight bushels per acre.
Payments are made on the basis of farm-to-farm inspections, and because it is recognized that harvesting is not always completed by September 15 it is regular practice to set a later cut-off date for final amendments to yield estimates. The date set for such filing was November 19, and written notice was mailed to every governmental body concerned on October 25. In other words, more than three weeks final notice was given to every responsible body that, if they had not made their application for P.F.A.A. payments and thought that they qualified for them, they had better get cracking with their amended estimates.
Yet despite the October 25 notice, several municipalities in Alberta have only recently submitted amended yield estimates, and have requested that now, at this late date, inspections be carried out in townships which up to November 19 were estimated to have wheat yields well above eight bushels per acre, many indeed as high as 18 or 20 bushels per acre. It does not seem justifiable to me that if farmers in these areas are now suffering hardships from lack of P.F.A.A. payments, the main burden of blame should be fobbed' off on the federal government.
I am sure every hon. member from the prairies understands, even better than I am beginning to understand, the problems involved in carrying out P.F.A.A. inspections at this late date. I am sure they know as well as I do how imperative it is that inspections be made as soon as possible after completion of harvest and before grain is fed to livestock or disposed of in other ways than through regular market channels.

The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Fane) also complained that the P.F.A.A. board of review had rejected certain areas recommended for payments in 1964. I would point out to him that it is the normal practice for the board of review-a three-man body with a farmer representative from each prairie province-to have the final say in deciding the eligibility of any area. I would also point out that the present members of the board of review, as well as the director and most of the field supervision staff, were appointed while the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) and the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) were the ministers. So I would hardly think that we could be charged with having any nefarious motives in this regard.
These are problems separate from the request of the Alberta government for federal financial assistance in a special relief program over and above P.F.A.A. payments for certain farmers in the Peace River and Rocky Mountain House areas.
It is true that the federal government has entered into arrangements for emergency farm assistance with four other provinces. I realize that this is an area in which no two judgments are likely to be the same. But it is our opinion that there are substantial differences in the circumstances of the aid program in the four other provinces and the proposal by the government of Alberta. In each case, these four provinces have never received P.F.A.A. assistance, with the exception of a very small area in British Columbia's Peace River district, while crop failure assistance has been available in Alberta and the other prairie provinces since 1939, to the extent, as I have indicated, of $189 million by way of federal contributions.
If the federal government contributed to the special assistance proposed by the province of Alberta, it would in effect mean increasing the federal contribution in two P.F.A.A. areas. There are other areas in the prairie provinces which have also had serious
292	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Greene crop losses but which have received only the standard P.F.A.A. payments. Our decision was based on the belief that it would not be equitable for us to add to the payments in one P.F.A.A. area without making the same assistance available everywhere.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
The Alberta government has proposed a special assistance program that could cost a total of $2.5 million. This is less than the $2.7 million the federal government has already committed, during the last three years, to farmers in the Peace River and Rocky Mountain House area under P.F.A.A.
The Alberta government has asked that we bear half the cost of assistance for farmers whose average yield over the last three years has not been more than 10 bushels per acre. But I would point out that there are some
7,000	townships under P.F.A.A. on the prairies and in the Peace River district of British Columbia and in approximately 10 per cent of these townships, or about 700, P.F.A.A. payments have been made in at least two out of three years, ever since the act was established in 1939.
If we gave this special treatment to two P.F.A.A. areas, what about the other 698 which have not received special treatment though they have known crop failure problems very similar to those now faced in the Alberta areas under question?
It has been suggested that our decision on this Alberta request is at variance with the assistance program offered in 1959. There is no similarity between the conditions on which the government's decision was based in this case and the conditions on which the government decided to offer assistance over and above P.F.A.A. payments in 1959. In the first place, the 1959 assistance was offered on the same terms to all three prairie provinces. What was offered to one P.F.A.A. area was available to all. In the present case, it would mean giving special treatment to these P.F.A.A. areas which is unavailable to all other P.F.A.A. areas.
In 1959, furthermore, many farmers were unable to harvest their crops in the autumn because of early snow which stayed all winter. As a result they were unable to determine whether they would qualify for P.F.A.A. payments or, if so, for how much, until they were able to complete their harvesting in the spring. The federal aid was offered in 1959 to help carry farmers in this situation through the winter until their P.F.A.A. positions could be determined. The provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan

agreed to share the cost of this assistance over and above P.F.A.A. payments eventually available to farmers. I would point out one fact with regard to this question which I think is particularly interesting: The province of Manitoba, however, shared in this assistance only as it affected farmers who could not qualify for P.F.A.A.
It was a firm condition of federal participation with each of these other provinces, New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia that this should be the last time such ad hoc assistance was necessary and that they would introduce crop insurance programs, in co-operation with the federal government to deal with such unavoidable production failures in the future.
As hon. members know there are special problems involved in devising a crop insurance program that will cover adequately the kind of mixed farming economy that exists in British Columbia and the eastern provinces. It is with these special problems in mind that the government plans to propose further changes in our crop insurance program during this session of the house.
But since 1960 the prairie province of Manitoba has found the federal crop insurance assistance of use to its farmers and it has found the federal program even more useful to its farmers after the changes introduced by this government in 1963. Yet it was not until last year that the province of Alberta saw fit to introduce crop insurance, and then only on a limited basis.
I think the current situation faced in Alberta, where there is a difference of opinion as to how an unavoidable judgment should best be exercised, is an excellent example of the weakness in continuing to take an ad hoc approach to this kind of farm problem, a farm problem which confronts governments in one form or another, and in some part of the country or other, every year.
I believe this is just one more strong argument for extending crop insurance to all of our farmers as quickly as we can. The farmers will then have available every year a foreknown and reliable means of providing for themselves, with substantial government assistance to relieve the cost of whatever degree of production security they feel is warranted.
There will also be a standard procedure to follow every year and in every farm area when production falters or fails. It will eliminate or at least reduce to a minimum the
January 26, 1966	COMMONS
need for exercising arbitrary judgments impossible of unanimous agreement, as is so obviously the case in the present situation.
That is all I have to say with respect to that subject. I should like to deal now for a moment or two with the speech made yesterday in this house by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) I thank him for the good wishes he expressed in my direction, as, indeed, I thank others for their good wishes including the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker). I trust I shall be worthy of them. Also of course I wish to thank the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) for giving me this opportunity for wider service to our country.
With regard to the speech made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, may I say first of all that I was disappointed at the slurring words he used in reference to the Prime Minister of our country. I think the services of the hon. member himself have been sufficiently distinguished as to make any reliance upon pettiness of this kind in making his contribution to this house unnecessary, and unworthy.

I represent one of those many regions in Canada where people are still fighting poverty and hunger every day, a region where agriculture is in complete stagnation. A few moments ago, I heard the Minister of Agriculture set forth his agricultural policy and I hope that he will have a kind thought for the farmers in Quebec, where they still have an average income of $3,000 per year. We approached the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) and we were accompanied by the present member for Saguenay (Mr. Blouin) and the member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Langlois). He told us that he did not see which act could force him to appeal to a company with a view to asking it to maintain its operations, its cruises.
The minister may be right, of course; there may be no specific legislation forcing him to intervene with the company. But we have been given to understand that, for the safety of passengers on board those ships, about $1 million would have to be spent on repairs. So, we have suggested that the minister provide, up to 1967 at least, grants which would enable Canada Steamship Lines to make those repairs so that our regions may also benefit from the legions of tourists which will be visiting the province of Quebec and Canada during the world fair.
Should the government refuse to intervene and should the company discontinue its cruises, it will of course be the end of the tourist industry in the Charlevoix and Saguenay areas and also in a large part of the district of Chicoutimi.
The representatives of municipal councils were so concerned about the matter that they wrote the following in a brief submitted to the authorities. I quote:
To cancel cruise ships in Charlevoix is to deprive the area of half of its tourist attraction, it is to deprive it of irreplaceable touristic publicity, it is to condemn it to touristic oblivion, and this, on the eve of the International Exposition on which we had pinned all our hopes.
In addition to the loss in tourist revenue, I must also point out that if those cruises are not resumed, from 500 to 600 persons will be laid off.
I think it would be one way for the Minister of Transport to launch his war on poverty to help settle this important problem.
During the election campaign Liberal speakers were telling us that the country was most prosperous and that there was nothing wrong with the country's economy. Immediately after the election came credit restrictions. Politicians, even those from Quebec, told us after restrictions were imposed on credit, that we had to tighten our belts, that times were hard.

The Address-Hon. M. Asselin
Municipal councils are greatly affected by these restrictions on credit imposed by the present government. I have already pointed this out in a question I put to the Minister of Finance, and he was supposed to inquire into the matter, but we have not yet received an answer.
Before the federal election, for instance, municipal councils had already obtained permission from the provincial and federal governments to go ahead with their winter works programs. They bought the materials and the projects got under way. But after the election, because of credit restrictions, chartered banks refused to lend them money to finance winter works on the excuse that they could not borrow from the Bank of Canada.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Some municipalities asked the government of the province of Quebec and even the federal government to deal with the problem, because a number of municipalities in the province of Quebec were forced to suspend their projects. Furthermore, while the members facing us say: "We are going through a period of great prosperity", some municipalities in the province of Quebec have to borrow from individuals in order to pay the people employed on winter works.
There are also municipalities in the province of Quebec which have not been able to carry out winter works this year because the federal government had not paid them the money which was due for last year. Mr. Speaker, that is the situation in our municipalities at present.
Because people in our areas are having a hard time and must work during the winter, I would ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), on behalf of our workers, to look into this situation as soon as possible in order to settle the matter without delay.
I should like to refer briefly to our amendment designed to raise old age pensions from $75 to $100 a month. Mr. Speaker, I did not expect that such an amendment would meet with any objections from government members.
During the election campaign, when our party proposed to increase the pensions, our opponents went one better on radio and television and on the hustings and said: "If the Conservatives can give you $100, then the Liberals can give you $125."
After all these fiery statements, how has it been possible for Liberal members, especially those from Quebec, to reverse their opinions

so rapidly? How will these members stand again at the elections and justify their sincerity? How will they be able to explain that the present federal government sends millions of dollars to underdeveloped countries, assigns millions to the storage of nuclear heads now obsolete, but refuses, on the other hand, an increase of $25 a month to our senior citizens, which would allow them to finish their lives in peace?

I do wish that our Liberals from Quebec will make the necessary representations for a revision of the family allowances scheme. It will be an excellent way for our colleagues to show us that they are really sincere when they talked about this famous war on poverty.
A question of current interest, Mr. Speaker, and one which has been referred to in the Throne Speech is that of federal-provincial relations.
During the past three years the federal and provincial authorities have met more than a hundred times to discuss the pension
January 26. 1966

plan, taxation, medicare and the war on organized crime. After each meeting press releases have been issued which, according to circumstances, reaffirmed either the firmness of the federal government or the autonomy of certain provinces in the fields of their respective jurisdiction.
But we must deplore, Mr. Speaker, that those meetings were used most of the time as a springboard for electioneering, blackmail and horse-trading, while dealing with such important matters as education, health insurance, and the fight against organized crime.
That those meetings be used to define the objectives, the aspirations and the rights of the parties concerned, this is understandable, but that they be used to make political capital, to make accusations and throw invectives against each other, such as those made by the Quebec Minister of Justice against the federal ministers and officials, when he called them spineless, such an atmosphere hardly contributes to strengthen national unity.
I know that all this is only a smokescreen, that after the provincial election, the relations between federal ministers and those of the province of Quebec will be friendlier than ever.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, to be hard on Ottawa, to appear as unbending autonomists is a profitable attitude to take in Quebec with provincial elections coming up. This is a kind of electioneering unacceptable in federal-provincial relations.
Let us then stop ad libbing and forging full steam ahead on constitutional matters of such tremendous importance for the future of our two ethnic groups.
Our constitution, Mr. Speaker, will soon be 100 years old. No one can claim it is doing well, that it is in excellent health. It is high time it were studied, revised, even altered and adjusted to the economic, political and cultural requirements of our two people. As for us, French Canadians from Quebec, we want to live with English Canadians as equal partners. We do not want to be considered as second class Canadians any longer, but as full Canadians. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first of all offer congratulations to you on your election to that post, important as it is to the function of this House of Commons. May I offer to you, sir, as Mr. Deputy Speaker, congratulations upon your election to that office. May I also take this opportunity to congratulate the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Goyer) and the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury).
It is with some reluctance, Mr. Speaker, even trepidation, that I rise for the first time to speak in this chamber, which has been referred to on different occasions as being the grand debating forum, the "grand inquest", of this nation. One who is new to this parliament must surely be impressed with its mere physical setting, its physical presence. One must also be impressed by the spirit which it seeks to represent and foster, the spirit of democracy, liberty, equality of opportunity, and so on, all of which can be synthesized into the overriding concept of justice, to the
300	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Schreyer end that this freedom, this equality of opportunity shall be made meaningful for all Canadians, or at least for the largest number of Canadians, rather than for a privileged few only. I presume that this is the ultimate objective of our efforts in this House of Commons.
Why do I take the time of this house, Mr. Speaker, to assert something which seems almost trite to say? I take the time to assert this because it is my feeling that such was not always the case in this chamber, only a few years or decades ago. We have made considerable progress, in my opinion, toward the objectives I have just mentioned. We have made this progress, by and large, in the economic sense at least, in the past two decades, with the advent of the modern, positive state in the post-war era. There has been growing acceptance of the idea or the practice that government is, and ought to be, used by the people, by the citizenry, by society, as an instrument to achieve certain social and economic programs, using the government to intercede in the economy to prevent specific abuses.
I refer, for example, to using government, through legislation, to reduce exploitation of the consumer by misleading advertising and packaging; to reduce wage earner exploitation by safeguarding the rights of employees through collective bargaining; and by legislating fair minimum wage laws which have substance and meaning.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
In the same way government can be used to enable farmers and other primary producers in this country to achieve fair prices relative to costs by means of farm price support programs, federal provincial marketing boards, crop insurance legislation, and so on.
This outlook on the role of government is finding increasing acceptance in our time, even though certain special privilege groups and, indeed, some well meaning individuals choose to attack it as creeping socialism, using that term of course as a term of opprobrium. It is ironic that often the very people who attack greater government involvement and responsibility on the philosophical plane are among the first to demand special payments, subventions, and the like, for depressed industries in their areas or for their constituents. It would seem that their philosophy of government depends on whose ox is being gored at any given time.

DEBATES	January 26, 1966
The process is a creeping and gradual one, admittedly, but it is a creeping forward of social awareness of and responsibility for individuals and groups of individuals who have in some way or another suffered dislocation because of changing economic conditions, illness, inadequate education, depressed sector prices and so on.
When one looks at this government's Speech from the Throne, its declaration of legislative intent, one must in fairness admit that it embodies much of the position of those who support the positive state idea-the idea of social democracy. But whether this government really wants to transform its intentions as set out in the Speech from the Throne, intentions which are presumably genuine, into actual law is another question. There's many a slip 'twixt the cup and the lip. We shall see in the course of the next few months what degree of success the government achieves in implementing its intentions and turning them into statutes. We shall see how steady is its hand.
Then too, there are some omissions and ambiguities in this Throne Speech which are remarkable, coming from a government which purports to be concerned with poverty, with low income regions and with low farm income. We heard the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) tell us this afternoon how much he wished that family farms would take their place in the economic sun. As I was saying, this is a government which purports to be up to date in its economic thinking and concerned with all these matters. But there are omissions. As an example I would refer to old age pensions.
There is increasing agreement in this country that $75 a month is really not sufficient in the light of present cost of living figures. Why does the government not agree to meet this problem head on? Apparently it is of the opinion either that the money is lacking or that an increase would somehow be inflationary.
The first opinion in my estimation reflects depression era economics. As to the second, that an increase might be inflationary, this comes even more strangely. What a strange way in which to fight inflation-by reducing the purchasing power of people on $75 a month. These people are already restricted enough in terms of what they are able to purchase.
Before I go on to other specific matters of criticism I should like to express agreement with this administration's reasserted intention
January 26, 1966

to make "O Canada" the national anthem. Drawing a distinction between national and royal anthems is done even in some kingdoms where the monarchy is indigenous. For Canada this is even more logical. I support it without equivocation and hope that the resolution of this question will not be used by any group to work ethnically divisive mischief, as was done during the flag filibuster.
Some words of commendation are also in order with respect to this government's intention to assume a larger share of the rising costs of education, particularly higher education. This can hardly be regarded as surprising. What is the alternative in the light of the soaring enrolment of students and the accompanying need for large scale construction projects on our campuses? If the government's statements about its desire to provide equal opportunity for all are to have any impact, could it do anything less than expand its educational assistance program so as to keep pace with the rising student population? Indeed it could be asked whether the size and scope of the federal aid recently announced is adequate.
I ask this question in the context of the current estimates of financial requirements in the field of education over the next ten years. It is expected that full time enrolment in our universities will treble in the coming decade. This will mean an increase of tremendous proportions in the number of university teachers, in teaching aids, laboratory equipment, lecture room space and so on. Those who are intimately connected with higher education, as I have had the privilege of being for a short period of time, have studied the problem in the past few years and estimated that the operating costs to universities in the current year alone will prove to be in the area of $420 million. Further, these sources estimate a capital expenditure amounting to about $800 million in relation to construction already under way or on the drawing board.
It is to these figures that the government's per capita operating grant must be compared. The increase in the grant from $2 to $5 is, of course, welcome. But it is evident that the approach taken toward the support of universities by the present administration is still, to quote from a brief to the federal government by the Canadian Association of University Teachers, "a series of ad hoc expedients" and without a sense of proportion. I submit that the federal government should adopt as its responsibility up to one third of the operating
The Address-Mr. Schreyer and capital costs of higher education. This need not and should not be considered as an impingement on provincial jurisdiction. It is consistent with the concept of co-operative federalism about which we have heard so much, particularly from senior ministers of this government.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Here is a golden opportunity to practise co-operative federalism in a field where there is some urgency that this be done, namely in higher education. In any case, Mr. Speaker, higher educational institutions like universities have, or should have the broader outlook, the broader goals that transcend provincial boundaries and jurisdictions. There is cause therefore for greater federal financial support, and I would think that there might be less opposition to this from the provinces than many on the opposite side may think.
I sat here this afternoon listening to the new Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) and since I am a representative for a constituency which includes a very large farming community, naturally I was interested in what he had to say. He spoke at some length about P.F.A.A., about its shortcomings, and about the extent to which it has been beneficial over the course of the past two decades. He seemed to know what he was talking about and he said what he had to say well.
The minister also made some reference to crop insurance and mentioned that it was going to be expanded. In that connection I would like to say that the crop insurance legislation which was enacted several years ago by the previous government was certainly much needed, and long needed by the farmers of western Canada. For that matter, it is needed by farmers in all parts of Canada. It was enacted by the previous government and they deserve credit for it. There can be no question about that.
However, it should also be said that the legislation as enacted then was not of much immediate value or benefit to the farmers of western Canada. It was not until the present Liberal administration passed certain amendments, which made it necessary for the provinces to reinsure back with the federal government, that crop insurance became really meaningful in western Canada, and it is now being expanded and made available to more and more farmers.
Earlier I said that there were some glaring omissions and ambiguities in the Speech from the Throne, and this is especially true as it
January 26, 1966

The Address-Mr. Schreyer relates to agriculture. In the ten page Throne Speech, this ten page declaration of legislative intent, there are to be found eight sentences about the Canadian farm scene. We are to understand that the government is going to expand the work of ARDA and increase its efforts to combat rural poverty. According to recent data it appears that about 40 per cent of Canada's rural population earns less than $3,000 a year, and these people are therefore regarded as living in poverty, if not deprivation.
That there should be such maldistribution of this nation's wealth, that there should be existing to this very day such obvious inequality of opportunity and purchasing power, is indeed a sad commentary on the past efforts or, rather, lack of efforts, on the part of successive Canadian governments.
So far we have been merely studying the problem of poverty-spending more on expertise than on the actual work of rehabilitation, retraining, up-grading, and providing farm product price supports. If the problem of poverty, and I am thinking now more particularly of rural poverty, is to be attacked in any meaningful way, it must include the idea of rural rehabilitation, of retraining programs for the displaced in rural Canada. It must also include at one and the same time a more meaningful farm commodity price support program than we have at present.
It was interesting to note that the other day the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), the minister responsible for rural development, and responsible also for ARDA, spoke on rural poverty to a luncheon meeting of business executives in Toronto. He was reported in the press as having shocked the honourable gentlemen at the luncheon with his forceful descriptions of the meaning of poverty in individual case studies that had been made.
It is not surprising that the minister should have been able to impress these people. I am sure he is quite capable of impressing people; I have heard him previously. But what is surprising is that these businessmen, these adult Canadians, should have been shocked by those accounts of poverty and its real meaning to individuals. Surely any adult active in public or business affairs has an awareness, has some knowledge of the existence of poverty

pockets of it, belts of it, regions of it, too much of it. Surely he has an awareness, indirect as it may be, of what this means in human terms to individuals caught up in the syndrome of poverty. Or, Mr. Speaker, are the upper income people in this

country so insulated and isolated from the way 40 per cent of their fellow Canadians live that they are shocked when they hear accurate descriptions of it?
Perhaps if the minister does some more shocking in the right places, this program of rural development and anti-poverty can go beyond the study phase toward actual combat of grievous income deficiency, and the causes of it.
But it would be wrong to think that all of this rural poverty problem can be eradicated through ARDA type programs, that is, through land use changes, land purchase and resale projects and so on, helpful as they may be. I maintain such projects can be effective, but only as an ancillary to an up to date price support program and marketing system for the agricultural industry. Without more adequate farm commodity price supports the task of reducing rural poverty facing ARDA is simply too immense, too overwhelming to be undertaken realistically.
There are too many Canadians with the misapprehension that low income farm operations are the result of improper land use, or smallness of size, or just plain inefficiency on the part of the farm operator. From my experience in provincial politics and provincial governments it seems to me that this misapprehension even permeates into the ranks of those connected with government, and therefore confusion is compounded.
Not enough attention has been focused by government people in the past-I am certainly not referring to farm organization people-on the issue of farm prices as being one major cause of rural poverty on the farms, as distinct from rural non-farm poverty. A more equitable pricing system and price support program for farm products would remove from the ranks of poverty, or from the brink of poverty, many farm families presently living on medium sized holdings.
I am not trying to say that all farm families can be brought up to desirable levels of income and standards of living by increased farm commodity prices, but many of them could be, and that is the point. Those whose farm operation is simply too small or too marginal to be aided materially could be rescued from their plight by the ARDA program proper.
It is difficult to quantify just what proportion of Canada's 95,000 low income brink-of-poverty families could be brought up to desirable living standards by means of more
January 26. 1966

realistic price supports, but it could be substantial. The more achieved in this way through the Department of Agriculture, the smaller and therefore the more manageable will be the task facing the department of rural development and its anti-poverty program.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
The tempo of change in the techniques of production has caused a dislocative social and economic impact on the lives of many people, particularly on this continent and in this country. In some industries this dislocation and potential dislocation has been eased by wise, sometimes altruistic, company management, by collective bargaining or by timely government legislation.
An excellent case in point can be found in the Freedman Industrial Inquiry report on C.N.R. run-throughs. This is a report submitted by Mr. Justice Samuel Freedman, a native son of Manitoba, of whom I think most Manitoba residents should be very proud. I will quote only one paragraph of this eminent jurist's report. Paragraph six of the summary states.
The commission is of the view that an obligation rests upon the company to take reasonable steps toward minimizing the adverse effects which a run-through-
I pause here to add parenthetically, or any other technological change. To continue the paragraph:
-may have upon its employees.
That obligation has its root in the principle that when a technological change is introduced the cost of reasonable proposals to protect employees from its adverse consequences is a proper charge against its benefits and savings.
In other words, what is being recommended here is that the cost of technological change be borne by those who benefit from it and not exclusively by those who suffer from it.
The same principle should be applied to our agricultural industry. Up to now this principle has not been honoured with respect to our farm people and the agricultural industry. In farming, technological change has been equally rapid. It has increased the productivity of Canadian agriculture with considerable benefit to the country. It is up to the rest of the population to reciprocate by supporting policies designed to ease the dislocation caused within the industry by this increased productivity and changes in technique.
The Address-Mr. Schreyer
I say in a somewhat bantering manner that perhaps this government should commission another Freedman inquiry-this time into the effects of technological change on the economics of family farm operations and the social responsibility arising therefrom. With his majestic command of language, perhaps this man and many others could see the problem in its true perspective. Thus far it seems obvious that very few men in power have either seen this problem or, having seen it, refused to acknowledge it.
Farm organization spokesmen and individual farmers in the past have been articulate in their explanations of the ills of their industry, and they have on many occasions advanced some possible solutions. Yet they have not succeeded in making much progress in impressing government. It is difficult to understand why, because they are not asking for unlimited price supports, or gigantic handouts from the public purse. One need only look at the briefs of the past few years and it becomes clear that they are asking for support on a limited or basic volume basis. They are asking for price supports, but on basic volumes of commodity production per farm operation. Surely this is the via media, the middle way, the golden mean-call it what you like, but it is the middle course they are asking for between the extremes of the price support policy in the United States-and it is extreme in many ways-and the extreme in Canada. In the United States there is no effective limit on the amount of price supports payable. The result is that big fat factory farms benefit more than those who need help most, the small and medium sized operator.
In Canada the extreme is in the other direction; a system of price supports that is almost entirely inadequate in every sense of the word. It seems clear to me and to anyone else who wishes to take a good look at the farming communities in Canada, including those in western Canada, that the standards of living of these farm families have not improved appreciably in the course of the past ten years. There are fewer farm families and there has been more consolidation, so it would seem to follow, or should follow, that the incomes of those left should be higher and better because they are larger in their operation. This is not true.
Ever since 1952 successive Canadian governments have either ignored the problems in agriculture or have tried to do something in a minor way, but have failed. There can be no
January 26, 1966

The Address-Mr. Schreyer other word but failure, because data collected by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics shows that the whole of agriculture has languished as a sector of low net income, while the rest of the economy of this country has grown, and it has grown at twice the rate.
Do members of this government seriously think that they will grapple successfully with the problem of farm income, as was the expressed hope of the new Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) this afternoon? Do they think they will grapple successfully with the problem of rural rehabilitation? Do they think the can do this successfully on the basis of an anti-poverty approach alone? I shudder at the prospect, because if this government tries to approach the problem of low farm income through anti-poverty programming, through purchases and resales of land, then there will simply be too many people who will then have to be retrained, too many units of land that will have to be bought up and resold for consolidation purposes; and this is too much.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in my place to speak in the debate on the Speech from the Throne. I wish I could say that we had started this new session of parliament with a dynamic program put forward by the government, in order to show that a minority government need not be a weak government, that a minority government might take the example of the minority government that we had in 1957, which put forward for the whole of Canada and its people the most dynamic program of development that this country had seen in 100 years.
I read through the Speech from the Throne carefully, looking for this kind of guidance. All I find is a collection of pious wishes, worn out cliches, talk of unity, brotherhood and co-operation. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this government has during the past three years done less for unity and more for division than any government we have had in 100 years.
So rather than going piecemeal through this list of empty, pious wishes, I should like this parliament and the people of this nation to return to that hopeful program of 1957, carried on through to 1963, when the government of the day had ideas, and the courage and the know-how to put those ideas into action.
Mr. Harry Hays, the late lamented Minister of Agriculture, had nothing to say on agriculture except that the previous administration had not gone far enough in its dynamic program for bettering Canadian agriculture. I am not going to take up too much of the time of the house in going through the long list of things that we did-but we made breakthroughs. I would remind the house particularly of our sales of agricultural products abroad. The "crimes" of 1959 and 1960 have now become the major virtues and claims for greatness of the Liberal administration. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) can get up and say, "We have doubled the sale of wheat" or, "We have tripled the sale of wheat"; but in 1959 and 1960 this was called treason.
They talk about improving crop insurance. Who put in crop insurance and made it available to the provinces? The Conservative government did. It is my lament that our own province of Alberta has not as yet taken full advantage of the federal laws regarding crop insurance, and although it is five years since they took it on in Manitoba, we still await

some program of adequate protection for the small farmers, the family farmers of western Canada and particularly of Alberta. Mr. Manning is not unaware of the problem, and just a few weeks ago he made what I thought was a fairly statesmanlike offer to the present administration to give some relief to the farmers of Peace River, Athabasca, Jasper-Edson and other constituencies in Alberta for their very serious and recurring crop damage. He has met so far with a stone wall; the federal government refused to co-operate. Yet they say we can look forward to renewed efforts on the part of the Liberal government to look after all people everywhere.
Although I am not at all against federal aid to undeveloped countries, help to our underprivileged friends in the commonwealth or in other parts of the world where they need help, I think it might well be time that we first looked at home to see whether or not our own people, the taxpayers and citizens of Canada, are being given adequate protection where they need it most. The way western Canadian farmers have been cynically neglected by the present administration is absolutely inexcusable. I believe the people of western Canada expressed undeniably their opinion of the present administration in the returns at the polls. However, this does not seem to have changed the government.
I should like to suggest to our new Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene), who comes from the east, that we in the west take no sectional view of the problems of agriculture. We welcome a minister of agriculture from any part of Canada, Mr. Speaker, who will listen to the farm organizations and to those people who are well able to assist him in his onerous task. If he does this, there is no reason at all why a minister of agriculture from the Ottawa valley, from the Annapolis valley or from any other productive valley in Canada cannot make a worth-while contribution to the welfare of this country.
There are many people who are ready to put agriculture on one side, throw up their

The Address-Mr. Bigg hands and say nothing can be done about it, and there is a great deal of talk today about making efficient family farms or enlarging acreages by buying up unproductive land, lending the farmers more money, enlarging their operation. Some say this will solve all the farm problems in Canada. It will not. It will add to all farm problems in Canada unless something else is done; that is, as my hon. friend over here in the corner just said, make sure that farm prices are stabilized, that the farmer who borrows money will have the opportunity to pay that money back, and that after he has paid it back he will still have enough left over to maintain the kind of living standard that we think Canada is well able to achieve.
This does not require socialism of any kind, and it does not require paternalism of any kind. It requires an administration that first sees that we have adequate markets both abroad and at home and then sees that it is possible for these farmers to get an adequate share of those markets. Nothing that the government has done, neither the Liberal administration nor the previous administration, has really had much effect upon agriculture beyond the fact that we established large and firm markets for our agricultural products. This is where we should put in our major effort. The farmers of western and eastern Canada are well able to supply these markets if we find the markets for them. Then they will be able to borrow money on their own, not from the government, not from the farm loan board but from any bank with any common sense; because if the farmer can make the money, they will be willing to make him a loan in order that he may make more money.
